## The idea

An eight-bar phrase can stop, pause, or turn aside depending on its last two
chords. Keep the melody and rhythm fixed and change only that boundary. V to I
lands at home. IV to I arrives with less pressure. A phrase ending on V hangs
open. V to vi aims for home and swerves.

A *cadence* is a conventional harmonic gesture at a phrase boundary. The four
behaviours above are authentic, plagal, half, and deceptive cadences. The names
are useful after the boundary types are audible. Before that, they risk becoming
four labels attached to silent arrows.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

chords = {
  I: chord(:c4, :major).to_a,
  IV: chord(:f3, :major).to_a,
  V: chord(:g3, :major).to_a,
  vi: chord(:a3, :minor).to_a
}

define :play_cadence_phrase do |chords, ending|
  body = [:I, :vi, :IV, :V, :I, :IV]
  (body + ending).each do |name|
    play_chord chords[name], release: 1.7
    sleep 2
  end
end

endings = {
  authentic: [:V, :I],
  plagal: [:IV, :I],
  half: [:IV, :V],
  deceptive: [:V, :vi]
}

endings.each do |name, ending|
  puts name
  play_cadence_phrase chords, ending
  sleep 2
end
```

The first six chords establish enough context for the endings to behave as
punctuation. Authentic and plagal both reach I, but V carries a leading tone and
stronger forward pressure. The half cadence stops on V. The deceptive cadence
shares two notes between I and vi, so the substitution is smooth and displaced.

## Change one thing

1. Remove the six-chord body and play each ending alone. Cadential identity
   weakens because a boundary needs preceding motion.
2. Hold the final chord for four beats. Duration can make an open harmony sound
   more deliberate, though the half cadence still lacks a return to tonic.
3. Put E in the bass of the final I chord. The authentic cadence retains its
   harmonic labels while the inverted tonic softens the arrival.

## Why it works

V contains B, the leading tone one semitone below C, and F is often added to form
V7. Those tones resolve inward to C and E. IV supplies F moving to E and A moving
to G, producing a gentler arrival. Both gestures rely on short voice movements,
but their approach chords create different tension.

The half cadence ends after the question has been posed. V is stable enough to
support a pause and directional enough to predict continuation. The deceptive
cadence exploits that prediction. Instead of C-E-G, it gives A-C-E. Two expected
tones appear while the bass moves elsewhere.

In code, a cadence is a two-symbol suffix appended to shared body data. That
makes the controlled comparison visible. The renderer knows nothing about
punctuation; it executes names. Meaning arises from order and tonal context.

Melody can confirm or resist the chordal ending. Put C above the final tonic and
the authentic cadence aligns bass, harmony, and melodic goal. Put E above it and
the harmony closes while the upper line feels less rooted. End the melody on G
and the chord is still I, though the top voice retains some openness. That is why
cadence labels describe a harmonic skeleton rather than every detail of the
heard boundary.

Tempo and spacing also affect perception. A two-beat silence after V may make a
half cadence feel like a deliberate question. Running immediately into the next
phrase can make the same V behave as an internal connector. Keep those timing
cues fixed during the four-way comparison, then vary them after the harmonic
categories are distinct.

## Take it further

Create a ten-trial cadence drill using the four endings. Begin with
`use_random_seed 42`, choose an ending, play the shared body and cadence, wait
four beats, then print the name. Use the same voicing and duration for every
trial. Keep a separate tally of confusions, especially authentic versus plagal
and half versus deceptive.
